interviewQuestions.question: What is a suffix array, and what does it let you do that a plain string scan can't?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A suffix array is the sorted order of every suffix of a string, stored as their starting indices rather than the suffix text itself. For `"banana"`, sorting all six suffixes alphabetically and keeping just where each one starts gives `[5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2]`.

Once it's built, checking whether any pattern occurs in the string becomes a binary search over the sorted suffixes — O(m log n) instead of an O(n) linear scan per query. That difference compounds when you're answering many queries against the same fixed text: you pay O(n log n) once to build the array, then O(m log n) per lookup, versus paying O(n) per lookup every single time with a scan.

Paired with the LCP (longest common prefix) array — the shared-prefix length between each pair of adjacent sorted suffixes — you also get the longest repeated substring for free as the maximum LCP value, and a route to the longest common substring between two different strings.

The honest caveat I'd add: I know what this structure does and roughly how it's built via prefix doubling in O(n log n), but I wouldn't claim I could derive an optimized from-scratch construction live under interview pressure — that's a recognize-and-apply topic more than a code-it-cold one.

**Testing:** whether you grasp what problem the structure solves and its complexity trade-offs, not whether you've memorized the construction algorithm byte for byte.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How would you find the longest repeated substring in a string, and what's the complexity?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd build the suffix array of the string, then the LCP array on top of it — LCP[i] being the shared-prefix length between the suffix at sorted position i and the one right before it. The longest repeated substring is simply the **maximum value anywhere in the LCP array**.

The reasoning: two suffixes sharing a long prefix means that prefix literally occurs at two different starting positions in the original string, which is the definition of a repeated substring. Sorting is what lets you only check *adjacent* pairs rather than every pair — sorted order guarantees the pair with the longest shared prefix always ends up next to each other.

Complexity: O(n log n) to build the suffix array via prefix doubling, O(n) to build the LCP array from it (using Kasai's algorithm, which I'd cite by name but wouldn't derive from scratch), then O(n) to scan for the maximum — O(n log n) overall, dominated by the suffix array construction.

The alternative — checking every pair of positions for a shared prefix directly — is O(n²) in the number of pairs times the comparison cost, so the suffix-array route is the one that actually scales to real string lengths. I'd name this as the textbook approach and note that competitive-programming versions push construction to true O(n) with more specialized algorithms, which I wouldn't expect to reproduce live.

**Testing:** whether you can connect the LCP array's maximum to the definition of a repeated substring, which is the actual insight being tested, not the construction mechanics.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Application

interviewQuestions.question: Why would you choose a suffix array over a suffix tree, given the tree offers faster O(m) pattern search?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because in practice the tree's asymptotic win rarely outweighs its real costs. A suffix tree is a trie built over every suffix of the string, with shared prefixes merged into common paths — real search is O(m), a full walk down the tree, versus the array's O(m log n) binary search. But that tree needs a genuine node-and-pointer structure, and construction to the optimal O(n) bound uses a non-trivial algorithm (Ukkonen's) that's meaningfully harder to implement correctly than prefix-doubling a suffix array.

Concretely: a suffix array is just an array of n integers — compact, cache-friendly, easy to serialize and reason about. A suffix tree over the same string can use several times more memory once you account for per-node pointer overhead, and that overhead actively hurts cache locality during traversal, eating into the theoretical search-time win.

So my default is the suffix array unless the specific workload genuinely needs the tree's O(m) search and can absorb its memory and implementation cost — for example, a system doing an enormous number of repeated pattern queries where shaving the log n factor off each search adds up, and where the engineering cost of a correct suffix-tree implementation (or an existing, well-tested library) is justified.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the practical engineering trade-off, not just recite the asymptotic comparison table.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You're building a code-search feature over a huge, mostly-static codebase and need fast substring lookups. Would a suffix array be the right call, and what would you watch out for in production?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes, roughly — a suffix array is a strong fit for exactly this shape: a large, mostly-static text corpus where you pay a one-time indexing cost and then serve many repeated substring queries fast. The "mostly-static" qualifier matters a lot here, though, because that's also the main thing I'd watch out for.

The first concern is **update cost**. A suffix array doesn't support cheap incremental updates — inserting or removing text effectively means rebuilding (or carefully patching) the array, an O(n log n) operation. If the codebase changes frequently, I'd either rebuild on a schedule (accept some staleness) or shard the index — build separate suffix arrays per file or module and merge query results, so a single file's edit only triggers a cheap local rebuild instead of touching the whole corpus.

The second is **memory at scale**. A suffix array over a multi-gigabyte codebase needs n integers each wide enough to index the full text — at real scale that's real memory, and I'd want to measure it against just keeping a simpler inverted index (tokens to file/line) for the common case of whole-word or whole-token search, reserving the suffix array specifically for substring queries that don't align to token boundaries (partial identifiers, arbitrary character sequences).

Third, cross-file search means building one suffix array over a concatenation of files with separators between them (same separator-uniqueness care as the Z-array), then mapping a hit's global index back to a specific file and line — that bookkeeping is easy to get subtly wrong and worth testing explicitly.

**Testing:** whether you can extend a data structure's textbook use case to a real system's constraints — staleness, memory, and multi-document mapping — rather than treating "suffix array" as a complete answer on its own.
